title: Marks (m, ')
instruction_text:
Marks let you jump instantly in large files!

KEY COMMANDS:
'm{a-z}' = set a mark at cursor position
"'{mark}" = jump to that mark's line
':marks' = list all marks

Your task: Navigate using pre-set marks!

We've placed marks in this file:
- Mark 'a' at line 4
- Mark 'b' at line 20
- ONE MORE hidden mark (find it!)

Steps:
1. Type ':marks' to see ALL marks
2. Find the third mark (besides 'a' and 'b')
3. Jump to mark 'a': type 'a
4. Delete 'DELETE_THIS' (press 'daw')
5. Jump to mark 'b': type 'b
6. Delete 'DELETE_THIS' (press 'daw')
7. Jump to the hidden mark
8. Delete 'DELETE_THIS' (press 'daw')
9. Save with :wq

THE BIRTH OF TEXT EDITORS: A JOURNEY THROUGH TIME

In the early days of computing, editing text was a tedious process. Programmers
worked with DELETE_THIS punch cards and paper tape, where a single mistake could
mean starting over from scratch. The concept of a text editor that could
interactively modify files on a screen was revolutionary.

The first text editors were line editors, requiring users to specify exact line
numbers for every operation. EDIT and TECO were among the pioneers, though they
were far from user-friendly. Users had to memorize cryptic commands and couldn't
see their changes in real-time. Imagine typing a command to change line 47 without
even seeing what line 47 contained!

The 1970s brought a revolution with the advent of video terminals. ed, created by
Ken Thompson for Unix, became one of the most influential line editors. Though
still command-based, it laid the groundwork for future innovations. Its successor,
ex, added more features and became the foundation for something truly special.

In 1976, Bill Joy created vi (visual) while working at UC Berkeley. This was a
game-changer: DELETE_THIS for the first time, programmers could see their entire
file on screen and move around freely! The modal editing paradigm - separating
command mode from insert mode - seemed strange at first, but it proved incredibly
efficient. Touch typists could edit at the speed of thought without reaching for
a mouse that didn't exist yet.

vi became the standard editor on Unix systems, beloved by systems administrators
and programmers worldwide. Its efficiency was unmatched - every command was
designed to minimize keystrokes. Want to delete a word? 'daw'. Delete a line?
'dd'. Copy five lines? '5yy'. The patterns were logical and composable.

But vi had limitations. It was tied to the original terminal interfaces and
lacked some modern features. In 1991, Bram Moolenaar started working on Vim
(Vi IMproved) to address these issues. Initially created for the Amiga computer,
Vim quickly evolved into a cross-platform powerhouse.

Vim added syntax highlighting, multiple windows, tabs, extensive plugin support,
and scriptability through Vimscript. It maintained vi's modal editing philosophy
while adding modern conveniences. The DELETE_THIS learning curve remained steep,
but the payoff was enormous - experienced Vim users could edit text faster than
seemingly possible.

The philosophy behind Vim is elegant: text editing is a language. Verbs (delete,
change, yank) combine with nouns (word, paragraph, line) and can be modified by
numbers and motions. This composability means learning a few commands unlocks
hundreds of combinations. It's why Vim users often say they "think in Vim."

Today, Vim remains one of the most popular text editors among programmers. It's
installed by default on virtually every Unix-like system. Modern editors like
VS Code offer Vim keybindings because the efficiency is undeniable. Even after
decades, nothing quite matches the speed and precision of a skilled Vim user.

The story of Vim is really a story about respecting the user's time and the
power of good design. Every feature serves a purpose. Every command is where your
fingers expect it to be. This is why people who invest time in learning Vim
rarely switch to anything else - they've discovered a tool that grows with them,
that never becomes a bottleneck in their creative process.

Whether you're editing configuration files on a remote server, writing code, or
crafting documentation, Vim is there - fast, powerful, and always ready. The
journey from punch cards to Vim shows how far we've come, and how some fundamental
principles of good software design remain timeless.
